I'm attending a community meeting in the Comunidad Ojo de Agua. Can you write what an elder might say about the water situation?

Nakatl Pascual Quispe Tika rises slowly. His breathing is labored — the doctors in Cerro Verde say it is from the dust.

'My grandparents told me the names of the springs. There were seven, once, and then as the years passed and the settlements came, five. When I was young there were still three. The water was cold and slightly bitter — we called it the taste of the mountain speaking. The llamas knew it. When you brought them to the water in the morning before the sun was full, you could see they were glad.

'In 2019 the first one went dry. We thought: a dry year. We waited. The second one went in 2021. The third in 2023. Now there is no morning water. We carry it from the town. Forty liters. In the old canisters that smell of plastic.

'They came, the people from the company, in 2012. They said: there will be prosperity, there will be work, there will be schools. They showed us papers. They said: we consulted you. Did they? We sat in a room in Cerro Verde. Someone explained things in Spanish very quickly. We signed our names. Is that a conversation? Is that consent? A man signs his name to a paper he doesn't fully understand and loses his water for the rest of his life. That is not a conversation. That is a trick.

'The flamingos are leaving. Last March, when we walked to the salar for the Fiesta, Nakatl Lucía counted the nests. There were fewer. There are always fewer now. The elders say: when the flamingos leave, the gods are warning us. I am an old man. I am not afraid to say: I hear the warning.

'The lawyers are fighting in Cerro Verde. The court said: reduce the pumping by fifteen percent. Fifteen. And still no spring water. The lawyers are fighting. We are carrying plastic canisters and listening to the wind where the water used to be.'
What might a young urban Zopikí professional say about navigating dual identity in Zoopaná?

Imagine a conversation with Luciana — 29, a software engineer at a tech company in Barrio Ceibo, Zoopaná, raised in the capital by parents from Comunidad Cerro Pasto:

'My parents came here in 2001, right after La Crisis — my father found work in construction, my mother cleaned offices. I was born here. My grandparents I saw once a year, for the August Festival, until my grandfather died. He spoke Zopikí. My mother understands it but doesn't use it easily. I understand maybe thirty percent.

'At the university — I studied at UPZ — I started the Zopikí language course. Not because anyone made me. Because I looked at myself in my third year and thought: I have a Quispe in my surname and I can't say fifteen words in the language my grandfather prayed in. That felt wrong.

'At work — we're a mixed team, mostly mestizo kids from Zoopaná and Puerto Marán, some foreigners. I've had to explain, more than once, that I'm Zopikí. People are always a little surprised. Like: you don't look like what they imagine. I've learned to let that go, mostly. What I don't let go is when people make jokes about the 'lithium problem' as if it's just a policy debate. I tell them: I have family near the Salar. The springs are dry. That's not a debate, that's someone's life.

'Do I have dual identity? Yes, obviously. I'm a Zoopaná software engineer and I'm Pequeéka-Zopikí. I listen to cumbia and reggaeton and also to Radio Zopikí online on Sunday mornings, which is when it plays the oral literature. Both things are true. Anyone who tells me I have to choose is making a demand my grandparents never would have made.'
Can you write a dialogue between a Cerro Verde resident who works at the mine and a Pequeéka community activist about lithium wealth versus water rights?

Setting: a kitchen in Barrio Tupanaku, Cerro Verde, after a community meeting.

MARCOS (40, Comunidad Cerro Pasto, has worked as a technician at the PCLT lithium processing plant for six years): The royalty. When the MGL passes — if it passes — two and a half percent goes to the Consejo. Do you know how much that is per year? At current production?

ROSA (35, Comunidad Volcán, FRZ sympathizer, her community's spring is still functioning but threatened by the proposed Salar del Volcán concession): I know the number. Twenty-eight million dollars. Per year. That sounds like a lot. It sounds like change.

MARCOS: It is change. For the schools in Comunidad Cerro Pasto—

ROSA: You're assuming the Senate passes it. You're assuming the governance structure works. You're assuming that two and a half percent of revenues from destroying our water is compensation. I'm not sure that math works for me. They took Pascual's springs. Can you put a price on that? Can you put it in the royalty calculation?

MARCOS: I know about Pascual. I know about the springs. I'm not saying the situation is good. I'm saying that my job pays for my daughter's school fees and my son's asthma medication — the medication he needs partly because of the same dust we're talking about, I know, I know the irony — and that if I choose between my family eating and the principle of the thing, I choose my family.

ROSA: I'm not asking you to quit your job. I'm asking whether the compensation we're being offered is proportionate to what is being taken. And whether there should have been a real choice before the first pump went in.

MARCOS: (pause) No. No, there should have been. That I agree with. The consultation in 2012 was a joke. I was 26. I remember my father coming home from that meeting and shaking his head. He couldn't explain what he had signed.

ROSA: That's the thing. That's all I'm saying. We start from there and we work forward. Not from 'the royalty is twenty-eight million' but from 'we were never properly asked.' Everything else follows from that.
What might an MZ politician say when explaining their coalition priorities to skeptical community members?

Imagine Diputada Rosario Cóndor Mamani speaking at a community assembly in Laguna Sal, after someone has challenged her about the MZ's presence in the Carballo coalition while the springs are still dry:

'I hear you. I hear what you're saying about Comunidad Ojo de Agua. I was there in March. I saw Nakatl Pascual carry a water canister. I know what those words mean: a person who has lived in the same community his entire life, who has drunk from the same spring his grandmother drank from, now carries plastic from town. I know.

'So let me tell you what the alternative is. Not what I wish it was — what it actually is. If the MZ leaves this coalition, President Carballo calls elections. In those elections, based on every poll I have seen, Ignacio Cruzat-Salinas Mendívil of the Partido Republicano wins. He will not pass the MGL. He will not accelerate the land titling. He will not keep Lic. Mamani Cóndor in the Ministry. He will not listen to VP Yahuar Huasi because there will be no VP Yahuar Huasi. He will continue extraction at full speed with no royalty provision and no water budget. That is the choice.

'The MGL is not everything we asked for. Two and a half percent is not three percent. The water enforcement mechanism is not as strong as what we wanted. The government is still appealing the precautionary measure through MINORSA's lawyers, which makes me furious — I will say that plainly. It makes me furious and I have said so in the chamber.

'But the MGL has passed the Chamber. If the Senate passes it, the Consejo receives twenty-eight million dollars a year that they control. New concessions require the Consejo's consent. The aquifer gets a legal budget. That is not nothing. In politics, not nothing is sometimes the difference between moving forward and losing everything you gained.

'I will keep saying this until the Senate votes: we are not asking for perfect. We are asking for real. Support us while we fight for real.'
A journalist asks Amaru Quispe Cari about the October 2025 blockade. What does he say?

'I want to be precise about my position, because I think you're looking for a fight between the FRZ and the Consejo that may be more dramatic than the truth.

'The Consejo Comunitario Pequeéka did not organize the October blockade. Tomás and the FRZ organized it. I respect Tomás. We came up in the same community — he's fifteen years younger than me, but I knew his family. The anger that produced the blockade is real anger. I share it. The springs are dry. The aquifer is going down. The flamingos are breeding at less than half the rate they were ten years ago. The precautionary measure gives us a fifteen percent reduction when we asked for forty percent and a full suspension. If I were twenty years younger and I had less gray hair and no particular position to maintain, I might have stood on the highway too.

'What I say about the blockade is this: it happened, the government had to respond, there was a meeting with Carballo, and for forty-eight hours the pumps ran quieter. Those are facts. Was it the right tactic? I don't think my opinion of the tactic is the most important thing. What matters is: are the communities better positioned after October than before? And I think the answer is yes, narrowly — because the meeting with Carballo forced the government to acknowledge us directly rather than through lawyers and ministry spokespersons.

'My approach is legal process and negotiation because I believe those are the instruments most likely to produce a durable outcome that the communities can sustain after I am no longer in this role. The injunction hearing is in August. If the court rules in our favor, that is worth more than a three-day blockade, because it cannot be appealed away as easily as a road closure can be cleared. If the court rules against us — then we have a different conversation.

'Sin agua, no hay litio. That hasn't changed. The method of saying it changes with circumstances.'
What would a Zopikí elder say to their grandchildren about why the March 3 commemoration matters?

'Come. Sit with me before the march. There is something I want you to understand before we walk.

'In our family there is a name we do not say out loud very often: Laguna Verde. Your great-great-grandmother survived it — she was six years old in 1879. Soldiers came at night to the winter camp. She was carried out by an older cousin and hidden in the grass. She never spoke about it when she was old. My grandmother told me once, quietly, that the woman had no words for it. Some things break the word-making in a person.

'For many years this was not something the Zoopan state admitted. For many years there were streets named for the general who ordered it. For many years the school books said: the Pacificación was necessary to open the land for civilization. As if we were weeds. As if the great-great-grandmother who survived Laguna Verde at age six was an obstacle to civilization.

'In 2004, finally, the government said: it was ethnic cleansing. The Congress voted. They built the memorial. They named March 3 a day of remembrance. This is something. It is not everything, but it is something that took generations of work by people who are dead now — Alcides Tupani Mamani, the teachers, the lawyers, the community organizers who wrote things down and refused to let the silence continue.

'Why do we march today? Not only to remember the dead. We march because the springs are dry. Because Nakatl Pascual carries water in plastic canisters. Because the flamingos are leaving the salar that your great-great-grandmother's people called sacred. The march connects these two things — the 1879 that broke the word-making in a six-year-old girl, and the 2025 that is drying the springs — and says: we are still here, we have not forgotten, and we are still fighting.

'Walk with me.'
Write a scene where a Pequeéka community member explains the salar's significance to a visiting journalist.

The journalist has driven three hours from Cerro Verde on a road that became a track that became a rough path. Nakatl Lucía Mamani Tupanaku meets her at the edge of what was once Ojo de Agua Primero.

'This is where the water was,' Nakatl Lucía says. She is 68, stands straight despite the altitude. 'See the discoloration in the soil? That was the edge of the spring. The water came from underground. Cold, always, even in summer. Tasted of salt and something else — the rock, the mountain. The llamas came here in the morning.'

'When did it stop?' the journalist asks.

'2019. It slowed first. We thought: a dry year. We have had dry years. Then one morning there was a small pool, then a damp patch, then nothing. The ground was the same color but dry inside.' She bends and picks up a handful of soil, lets it fall. 'The second spring went in 2021. The third in 2023. Now we walk to town.'

The journalist asks about the salar's spiritual significance. Nakatl Lucía pauses.

'I will explain it in the way that can be understood. For you, a church is a building. If someone destroys the building, the faith can continue in another place. For us, the salar is not a place where we perform ceremonies. The salar is itself the living body of something sacred. The flamingos are not symbols of the sacred — they are themselves sacred. The water is not a resource — it is a being with which we have a relationship of reciprocity that goes back to our ancestors.

'When the flamingos stop breeding, it is not that we have lost a beautiful bird. It is that a relationship of reciprocity has been broken. Our obligations and their obligations are no longer in balance. That is a spiritual emergency. I am trying to tell you this in a way that a newspaper can print. I don't know if it is possible. But try to print it honestly.'

She looks toward the salar.

'The lawyers are fighting about aquifer data. I am glad the lawyers are fighting. But what they are fighting about, ultimately, is this: the right of this ground to remain what it has always been. That is what Sin agua, no hay litio means. Without the water, the relationship is broken, and broken relationships have consequences that no court can fully calculate.'
What might someone at the Cerro Verde March 3 march say to the crowd at the Mirador del Salar?

At the Mirador del Salar, the crowd of 10,000 looks down at the white geometry of the evaporation ponds spreading across the salar floor below. A young Pequeéka woman from the FRZ takes the microphone:

'Below us you can see the ponds. One hundred and forty-three years ago today, Barros Uribe signed the decree that sent the army into our communities. One hundred and forty-three years. And here we are still, on this hill, looking down at something that was done to our territory again without our consent.

'I was asked today: aren't you glad the government recognized the Pacificación? And I said: yes. I am glad. It matters that the CHIZ report exists, that the memorial exists, that the curriculum mandate exists. I am glad for Ley 8.127/2004 and I am glad that our VP says our language in the Senate. I am not going to pretend these things are nothing.

'But look down there. Look at the evaporation ponds. The springs in Comunidad Ojo de Agua are gone. Three springs that our people drank from, that our llamas drank from, that our ceremonies used — gone. The government formally recognizes what was done to us in 1879. And in 2013, it licensed the same thing in a different form, and in 2025 it is appealing in court the precautionary measure that would have slowed the damage.

'We are not ungrateful for what has been won. We are awake to what has not been won.

'The injunction hearing is in August. The MGL vote in the Senate could happen any week. Our lawyer Dr. Valentina Cóndor Quispe is fighting. Amaru is negotiating. We are marching. These are different hands reaching toward the same thing: a future in which our children inherit water, not just a memorial.

'Sin agua, no hay litio. Sin tierra, no hay justicia. Without water, no lithium. Without land, no justice. We will be back on this hill next March 3.'
What is Nakatl Rosa Cóndor Volcán's view of the possible development of Salar del Volcán?

Nakatl Rosa Cóndor Volcán, the community leader of Comunidad Volcán, has been the most uncompromising voice among the Pequeéka leaders on the question of the Salar del Volcán. She spoke before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in its 2024 session, and her statement has circulated widely: 'If they pump the Volcán, the flamingos leave and the gods leave with them. That is not negotiable.' In extended conversations with journalists and advocacy organizations, she has elaborated this position with precision. The Comunidad Volcán, approximately 840 people, herds traditional llamas on seasonal wetlands fed by volcanic springs near Volcán Tupanaku — the dormant volcanic vent at the northern edge of the Salar del Volcán. The flamingo breeding colony on the Salar del Volcán is approximately 1,200 pairs — a significant population that BirdLife International has designated as conservation-critical. From Nakatl Rosa's perspective, the Comunidad Volcán has watched what happened to Comunidad Ojo de Agua — a community whose springs dried within four years of nearby brine pumping beginning — and they regard that as a preview of their own future if concessions are granted on the Salar del Volcán. She has stated formally that the Consejo Comunitario Pequeéka Volcán sub-council will not provide FPIC consent under any circumstances, regardless of royalty offer or community benefit package. She does not characterize this as anti-development: 'You can develop the lithium on the salar that is already consigned. We are talking about a different salar. Leave it.' The MGL's FPIC provision, if enacted, would give the Consejo the legal right to make this refusal binding.
How does an urban Zopikí voter in Zoopaná think about the March 3 commemoration versus the daily water crisis in the communities?

The perspective of urban Zopikí Zoopans on the relationship between the commemorative framework and the living crisis is revealing about the complexity of indigenous political identity in the capital. For second-generation urban Zopikí voters — raised in Zoopaná, perhaps with grandparents from the Sierra del Oeste — the March 3 commemoration at the Memorial de la Pacificación del Sur is often experienced as the primary site of active indigenous identity engagement. It is personally meaningful: the memorial architecture is powerful, the ceremony is dignified, the recognition is genuine. But the salar water crisis is geographically distant in a way it isn't for someone in Cerro Verde looking down at the ponds from the Mirador. For these voters, social media has changed this distance: the #ZopikíVivo content stream regularly surfaces photographs of dry spring beds, videos of Nakatl Pascual carrying water canisters, data from Dr. Mamani Cóndor's aquifer measurements. The communities that once felt far away are now visible in the feed. This has re-engaged urban Zopikí political identity in ways that the commemorative framework alone didn't always accomplish. The pattern in Zoopaná precincts with high Zopikí-heritage population: the 2023 election saw MZ's urban vote share rise from 38% to 45% — driven partly by VP Yahuar Huasi's candidacy and partly by the salience of the lithium conflict. The March 3 commemoration is the institutional occasion; the water injunction and the flamingo crisis are the living proof that commemoration alone is insufficient. Urban Zopikí voters hold both of these in mind simultaneously and, increasingly, are showing up for both.
Can you write a brief scene of a community meeting where the Pequeéka royalty is being discussed?

Community hall, Comunidad Cerro Pasto. Evening. About sixty people present. Nakatl Félix Tupani Cóndor is facilitating. A printout of the MGL summary in Zopikí and Spanish is taped to the wall.

WOMAN IN HER FORTIES (a nurse who works at the Cerro Verde clinic): I want to understand the royalty number. Twenty-eight million dollars per year — is that for all fourteen communities? Or just for the four of us near the salar?

FÉLIX: The MGL says for the Consejo Comunitario Pequeéka, which represents all fourteen communities. The Consejo would have to create a distribution mechanism.

MANIN HIS THIRTIES (works at PCLT; his wife is from Comunidad Ojo de Agua): So each of us — nine thousand people? That's three thousand dollars per person per year. If they distribute it equally. That's real money.

OLD MAN IN THE BACK: Three thousand dollars does not give Comunidad Ojo de Agua their springs back.

Silence.

FÉLIX: He's right. The royalty and the water question are not the same question. The MGL also has the water budget provision. Both have to pass together for either to mean what we need.

WOMAN WITH A CHILD ON HER LAP: And if only the royalty passes? If the Senate cuts the water budget provision?

FÉLIX: Then the MZ says we pull our support. That's the coalition line.

MANIN HIS FORTIES (skeptical): The MZ has said before what it will and won't accept. And then it stays in the coalition anyway.

What I can tell you is that on this specific provision — the FPIC clause and the water budget — Diputada Cóndor Mamani and VP Yahuar Huasi have both said publicly, on record, that these are non-negotiable. Whether that holds — I don't know. What I know is that without the royalty and the water budget together, we are in a worse position than we are now. The springs are dry and we have nothing.
